subsubtopic: LONG-RANGE RADIO NAVIGATIONAL SYSTEM-CALL FOR EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's current non-directional beacon air navigation system places Canada in the steam age of flight. In this day and age air travel is a necessity, and all parties involved in this mode of transportation, including our federal Government, should be concerned with increasing air safety.
The Loran-C, long-range radio navigational system, is well proven and is a highly accurate system whose service, if extended, would increase air safety across the country. The aviation management committee of the Roads Transportation Association of Canada recently passed a resolution supporting the expansion of the Loran-C system. This system has the support of the provinces and the territories. The United States is currently testing Loran-C, with the U.S. National Association of State Aviation officials campaigning for its adoption.
With 55 per cent of flights in this country made below 5,000 feet altitude, and 58 per cent made under visual flight regulations, how can the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and his Department be strongly considering the Omega VLF system which is too expensive for the majority of general aviation pilots to consider?
The provinces see the need to adopt the Loran-C system. It is time for the federal Government to wake up to this need and improve air safety in Canada by extending the Loran-C system.

I am speaking, Mr. Speaker, about the lack of enforced no-smoking areas in our parliamentary restaurant, our cafeterias, our committee and caucus rooms. subsubtopic: MUTUAL BALANCED VERIFIABLE NUCLEAR WEAPONS FREEZE PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the very time President Reagan and General Secretary Gorbachev were meeting in Geneva, Canada failed once again to take up an opportunity to break the momentum of the nuclear arms race. At the United Nations First Committee, Canada voted no to a mutual, balanced, verifiable nuclear weapons freeze. Like the Liberals before them, Conservative Members continue to reject the almost universal call for the nuclear superpowers to freeze the testing, development, and deployment of nuclear weapons.
This year at the First Committee, our friends, including Australia, Norway, Denmark and New Zealand voted in favour of a freeze. A total of 113 countries supported the freeze and only 11, including Canada, voted against it. Despite the fine words of peace of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)
November 22, 1985

and the earlier record of Canada's Disarmament Ambassador who supported a freeze when he was a Conservative Member of the House only two years ago, Canada has failed to take even this modest action to halt the nuclear arms race.
Canada can and must do more for peace than send the Prime Minister to Brussels to be debriefed by President Reagan. It is time for initiative and action. At the very least Canada should support the initiatives being taken by others at the U.N. and elsewhere. I urge the Government to change its vote when the freeze issue comes before the General Assembly of the U.N.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF AIRLINE DEREGULATION IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Dennis McDermott, President of the Canadian Labour Congress, made a statement on CTV's Question Period on Sunday to the effet that the recent increase in air accidents in the United States occurred as a result of its deregulation of the airlines. I feel that he is exploiting the public's natural fears regarding air safety, either in the cause of some personal vendetta or on the basis of a total lack of understanding of a very complex problem.
No union head in the United States has made statements comparable to those made by Mr. McDermott. Perhaps he is not aware of the fact that deregulation will create many new jobs in safety and in operations, and will bring flying within the reach of millions more Canadians.
The fact is that there has been no increase in accidents involving fatalities in the United States, or elsewhere in the world, in spite of our pereceptions based on the two recent tragic and terrible crashes and the fact that traffic has increased greatly. However, the United States is under fire for having failed to increase its safety facilities and personnel in proportion to increase traffic. I can tell Mr. McDermott that we will not make the same mistake.
Our record since partial deregulation over a year ago shows no increase in accidents in spite of increased airline activity. A perception of increased accidents has probably arisen because what are called incidents or near-accidents have been reported mandatorily since last June. As well, we are even now in the process of designing supplementary new radar equipment to improve air safety. Safety has been and remains our number one priority.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO BUILD MICRO-CHIP RESEARCH CENTRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the future success of practically all Canadian businesses will depend on their ability to develop or adopt innovations based
on semiconductor technology. It is in this context that the Canadian Micro-electronics Corporation submitted its business plan a few days ago. The plan recommends the building of two advanced microchip research centres with the main purpose of training engineers and scientists in leading edge semiconductor technology.
The CMC plan calls for $155 million to be spent over five years to set up two centres designed to work on advanced silicon production techniques and process technology. Technology developed through these centres will be translated into the creation of wealth and new jobs. Economic analysis shows that 100 jobs in semiconductor research and development lead to over 31,000 jobs in the rest of the economy.
I urge the Government to consider favourably the proposals of the CMC. Investment in intellectual capital now will have high returns for our country's economic well-being and will enhance productivity and create new industrial opportunities. The business plan recommends Ottawa-Carleton as the best location for one of the research centres. I applaud this choice and strongly recommend that the Ottawa-Carleton region be considered for one of the facilities. It has the right infrastructure and expertise at hand to meet the challenges set by the microelectronics industry.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE (TOURISM)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, knowing the interest in tourism of Hon. Members on both sides on the House of Commons, I am pleased to have the opportunity to report briefly on the results of the fortieth federal-provincial conference of Tourism Ministers held this past Tuesday and Wednesday in Vancouver. Hon. Members are undoubtedly aware that the meeting was the culmination of an extensive public discussion and consultation process which has taken over a year to conclude. That consultation process involved all the provincial and territorial Governments, all the major tourist associations and literally thousands upon thousands of Canadians.
The Government said from the outset that Canada's economic growth would be best achieved through a co-ordinated effort by the public and private sectors. The Vancouver meeting demonstrated a joint effort by all the levels of Government to respond to the advice that we received from the private sector. One result was a detailed statement of principles regarding the roles and responsibilities of the provinces, the Territories and the federal Government with respect to tourism.
By setting out their positions and views, Governments enabled the private sector to take directions in the full knowledge of the framework in which it operates. For our industry, this framework sets out the guiding principles for marketing and particularly consumer advertising and indicates that both orders of Government have a role to play.
The agreement also sets out specific actions for both orders of Government in research and the development of a Canadian product. It emphasizes that consultations among the various partners are essential and will take place. Finally, our agreement outlines government repsonsibilities in terms of the awareness of the general public and of visitor reception to this grand and glorious country of ours. Our agenda did not attempt to set out every action for every Government in Canada. What it did set out was a framework for doing business together in the future. That was but one accomplishment.
Knowing as I do the importance of the tourism industry to so many Canadians and indeed to so many Members of the House of Commons, I am pleased to say that the Government responded specifically and positively to the major recommendations put forward by the private sector over the consultation process. Those recommendations were for marketing, training, product development and research. Understandably, Canada's image abroad was the area of most interest throughout the consultations. We are all concerned of course about how others see us.
As Hon. Members will be aware, the Government has commissioned the largest tourism study ever carried out in the United States, our largest potential market. Its results are
Statements by Ministers
nearly all in and early next year, as I have assured my provincial and territorial counterparts, the information will be made broadly available not only to Governments but to industry and generally to any Canadian who would want it. The Government believes that one of our tasks is to ensure that accurate data is made available to our industries so that they can be best equipped to make the business decisions necessary to carry the industry forward.
At the Vancouver meeting Ministers also agreed that a more specific marketing campaign than those which have been held in the past is essential. The market-place is changing rapidly and dramatically and marketing programs have to respond to that reality. I assured my counter-parts that the federal campaign was developing along the lines suggested by them, which indicated a greater emphasis on destination and product-specific advertising which, of course, coincides with the research we have obtained over the past number of months.
Further, we agreed to consider how to involve the provinces and the Territories in the American launch of the federal marketing program which will commence in early 1986. Responding to the private sector's advice that a better coordinated marketing effort is needed in the international market-place, the Ministers agreed in principle to create an advertising council with both government, public and private sector members. The precise role and operations of the council will be developed over the next month or so; but the broad intent is to have Canada's major players who are involved in the international marketing of tourism to meet regularly in order to discuss their own plans and to comment on the plans of others. Hence, this will give us all a better understanding of the direction which we should be taking in terms of our international marketing. I believe this is a major step toward coordinating our efforts and perhaps in the long run toward integrating our various marketing campaigns.
Consultations suggested that the Canadian product line had to be improved and extended. In response, Ministers agreed that making more extensive use of Canada's cultural industries would be a major improvement. The rich mosaic of the country is one of Canada's most appealing qualities, both to the international traveller and buyer and to our own domestic consumers. Over the course of the next short period of time we will hold discussions with members of the arts and cultural communities across the country, with multicultural groups and, of course, with native cultural groups to ascertain how we can improve the role which we see as being important and how we can co-ordinate it. As has been mentioned, we will discuss setting the particular aspect of our unique land forward for our visitors to see.
I believe that the commitment to the tourism industry by the federal, provincial and territorial levels of Government has been made abundantly clear by the signing of subsidiary agreements valued at some $375 million. There can be no doubt that the Governments firmly believe in the economic potential of this industry, one which employs 600,000 Canadi-

November 22, 1985
Statements by Ministers
ans and which generates economic benefit in the neighbourhood of $18 billion to $19 billion per year. I believe we have made significant progress over the past year in addressing the issues affecting the tourism industry.
I would like to take this opportunity to recognize the major efforts of my provincial and territorial colleagues, both in respect of their own jurisdictions and in support of federal efforts. The meeting was a good one. I can inform Members of the House that federalism in the country is alive and well. I have never seen a group of politicians from all poitical Parties work together as well as we did this past week.

Their advice went well beyond narrow interests. We have completed the major phase of our work, which was set out in September of 1984 which, in some respects, was a redirection of our industry.
We are now well prepared to enter the second phase which is, of course, the implementation process. However, consultation is and will remain a cornerstone of how the Government operates. I can assure all Hon. Members, and through them the industry interests that each of them represents, that 1 will continue to seek counsel and advice from all corners of the House of Commons and from all parts of Canada. It can be said to all those involved in the past process that significant progress has been made, progress resulting from joint efforts of the public and the private sectors. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on a matter of great interest to me, tourism. The report the Minister has just made does have positive aspects. What strikes me most is the Minister's intention to maintain consultations with the tourist industry. It would have been unthinkable to exclude the private sector from the decision-making process. In my estimation, the Minister's initiative as a whole is a step-I repeat, a step in the right direction, but I dare hope he will eventually go beyond the consultation stage and take action.
I should like to remind the Minister of his own remarks to the tourism conference delegates hardly a month ago.

This conference will achieve results. I expect you to give clear choices and make hard recommendations to me and my provincial colleagues .. . tourism's voice is really starting to be heard and this conference is a key opportunity for you to speak out before we convene in November to take the decisions that will give further direction to the industry. We will make the decisions that are needed.
I must say that hard decisions or hard recommendations were made at this conference but were not adhered to at the provincial-federal conference.

The Minister must wish he could take back his fine words which, in fact, did not cause much of a ripple in Vancouver. Truth to tell, I am disappointed but not surprised, for after all the Minister has the same shortcomings and feels the same pressures as his Conservative colleagues. One day they make tantalizing promises, the day after they conveniently forget them. It is a hazardous game which seldom fails to backfire. I have a telling example of that, Mr. Speaker, and I imagine that Members opposite still recall when they were on this side of the House. Be that as it may, we should not be overly concerned if some of them have a short memory, they will soon have an opportunity to sit across the way. It being so, I would like to remind them-and the Minister should indeed lend an ear-of the Progressive Conservative Party's position respecting tourism.
The present Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport and Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek), who was in the House a few minutes ago, will certainly be familiar with his own statements. Here are some of them:
Unfortunately the Minister did not come to grips with the major problem of the Canadian tourist industry, namely excessive taxes on hotel and restaurant services as well as on gas and alcoholic beverages which are driving the industry to bankruptcy.
Here is another one:
By freezing at their current level all taxes which are harmful to tourism and seeking ways to reduce them in certain sectors ... in our capacity as politicians we have to realize that we cannot raise taxes without first knowing what their impact will be. We must stop milking businessmen for all they are worth.
And a third:
By taking " ... steps to tackle the bane of tourism-overtaxation."
Mr. Speaker, I have many more such quotations and I could go on putting them on the record.
And I will continue with a quote from the Party Leader, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), of course, who promised during the election campaign that he would:
Review taxes on gas, alcoholic beverages, food and accommodation that are making Canada's tourist industry less competitive.
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note how concerned the Conservatives were then about our tax system.
Those same Conservative Members have now made a sudden about-face. Today they are saying the exact opposite of what they said before, and worse, they are trying to evade the subject. This is not the way things are done, and the party now in power has no right to deal with the tax problem in this frivolous manner.
The Minister has repeated time and time again to the tourist industry that taxation is not a problem. Easy to say for him, but it just shows he refuses to face reality. Our taxes are too
November 22, 1985

high here in Canada, and that is a serious problem. There are no two ways about it. It is as plain as the nose in your face. I do not understand why the Minister keeps turning a blind eye to this fact. You advised the industry to submit recommendations before the minister's meeting in Vancouver. These recommendations included one that was repeated many times, and that was to restructure the tax system.
At this point I would like to quote the President of the Canadian Association of Restaurant and Food Services, Mr. Robert Degrace, who, in concluding, warned the Minister at the national conference:
At this Conference ! have heard that cost is not a significant competitive factor. I want to tell you that it is, Mr. Minister. When are we going to look at the tax structure in Canada and their impact on the price of tourism services?

The Minister will agree that the message was clear. In any case, one cannot deny reality. Canadian products are becoming less and less competitive with American products. Even with our devalued dollar, we are still losing. First of all, if we look at the price of gas, which costs from 25 to 30 per cent more in Canada than in the United States. And then-
Is there a time limit, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as spokesman of the New Democratic Party for Tourism. I am pleased this afternoon to reply to the Hon. Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Murta).

I would like to begin by saying, Mr. Speaker, that we appreciate the Minister's initiative in reporting to the House on this meeting with his provincial and territorial counterparts. The general direction of the Government's efforts in promoting tourism within Canada is, of course, one thing which, like motherhood and apple pie, is not very easy to question. The consultation process, indeed, has a great deal of potential in terms of unifying the efforts of different levels of Government and in moving the country's industry in a single direction, one which will, hopefully, benefit all parts of the country and all the Parties represented at such conferences.
Nevertheless, there are significant problems with the consultation and inter-ministerial process. These are problems which are worthy of remarking upon in this House. My understanding of the Accord is that it is largely a rewriting of the 1980 Accord which was signed in Saskatchewan, and while the consultation process, as I have said, has great potential, we must, of course, over the months and years to come, look for some realization of that potential and some achievement which can be directly traced to what after all is an expensive process in time and effort.
The Conference which was held here in Ottawa, I believe, last month, attracted considerable participation from the private sector. I would caution the Government that participation is not something which can ever be taken for granted. 1 am very glad to hear the Minister thanking the private sector for coming along in significant numbers and making a contribution. However, I caution the Government that unless there are results from such a process, the commitment of the private sector will diminish. The private sector, naturally, is looking for favourable results for the industry.
Frequent mention was made at that particular conference at which 1 attended several sessions-and I was grateful to the Minister for the invitation to do so-of the study which is presently being carried out in the United States, our largest market and presumably continuing to be so. The study was based on interviews and was done in considerable depth. The results will be shared throughout the industry and with our provincial partners. I think that such a study has great potential for revealing the reasons our American friends come to Canada in significant numbers, but it also has some potential pitfalls which 1 believe the Ministry would do well to review. I am afraid that when that size of a project is set in motion, it generates a sort of halo effect, an interest and receptiveness which might not necessarily be there when we come to the real life situation of making those hard choices and decisions as to where the holiday makers' earnings are going to be spent. For this reason I think the Ministry would do well to try to apply

November 22, 1985
Statements by Ministers
some control to those interviews and to review whether or not the results obtained are somewhat coloured by the very intimate and attentive manner in which the basic data is being gathered.
Turning to advertising, I am glad to see the Government's commitment to advertising in the international market. The previous Minister of Tourism made some good points when he made a critical review of some of the previous advertising. However, my understanding is that the 1986 Budget has been almost totally committed to international advertising, and if there is a lesson to be learned from the geography of our country, surely it is that we cannot take it for granted that Canadians are aware of the full range of attractions in their own country. We cannot take it for granted that Canadians will automatically consider Canadian destinations which might very well fill the needs and values that they are looking for in their vacation experience. Increasingly, of course, with the lifting of the ceiling on airfare taxes and the rise in the gasoline tax, we cannot assume that Canadians can afford to visit other parts of their own country.
I am glad to see that the conference produced an emphasis on the potential of Canadian culture to attract visitors. As one who represents more Indian people and certainly more reserves and bands than any other Member of this House, I was also pleased to see the emphasis on the involvement of native Canadians in tourism and not simply on exploiting them. Much more important, we are ensuring their participation and a fair share for them in the benefits from the tourism industry. However, I feel there are a couple of cautions which have to be made here. I do not think the traditional values of Canadian tourism and its attractions can be discarded. They have to continue to be emphasized.
[Translation}
When we review the main tourist features of Canada, we notice that moose, red-coated police officers and mountains attract a great many visitors from the United States, as well as countries of Europe and the Far East.

These are factors which cannot be ignored and must continue to be emphasized. Therefore, as I said to the previous Minister of Tourism before he was appointed Minister of the Environment, it is important that there be considerable coordination between those two Ministries to ensure that our national parks continue to provide a refreshing and innovative recreational experience of quality at affordable prices, without excessive barriers involving fiscal or non-fiscal control such as the rationing of visitors to national parks. We have had a commitment from this Government to increase training in the industry. That is good but it has to be put into concrete terms through funding because, by and large, it is fair to say that as a large country we do not have that intense awareness of tourism which our European competitors do.
My colleague from Westmorland-Kent addressed the problem of taxation and it is a very considerable one. The Government has not put into motion any form of study to determine whether the tourism industry does, as has been alleged, bear a disproportionate tax burden in relation to the total economic activity in the industry. The barriers to tourism which we have are large. They are large by virtue of geography, awareness, and by virtue of the fact that this country presents very disparate and different images. Let us see a Ministry which ensures that those barriers are not increased by making Canadian tourism non-competitive from the point of view of price.

If this clause passes in its present form in the Bill as it is reported from committee, we will have enshrined a precedent in how we treat certain private companies in this country. To my knowledge and the knowledge of the legislative committee, there is not a single other example of a 25 per cent limit in existence in any legislation concerning private sector companies in this country. Indeed it would be the first time that such a procedure would be put into effect.
We believe that rather than put this new precedent into the books, we should look at the cases where we presently restrict private companies in certain ways. For instance, the figure used for the banks is 10 per cent. No individual or corporate group can have a holding larger than 10 per cent of the over-all shareholding. Therefore, we have moved this amendment to achieve that same kind of limited corporate partnership entry into CDC.
We do this for a number of other reasons besides consistency. First, the President of the CDC himself indicated that this would be best for the company. Second, we are concerned with a process which has taken place by which close to 15 per cent of the shares in this company have already come under the control of the Brascan group which has clearly indicated from its past that it is interested in restricting competition in an arrangement with the Kidd Creek mine which CDC owns.
In addition, it is quite possible that a situation could develop with a 25 per cent shareholding. We in the committee asked our witnesses about this and they told us what could happen when a company had a 25 per cent shareholding. A company like Brascan-we should be aware that Brascan played a major role in the shaping of this legislation-would be able to establish such a paralysis within the company itself that CDC would be forced to sell off the Kidd Creek mining properties to Brascan, in which it has always had such interest, in order to placate a partner that was not prepared to co-operate.
A partner that has only 10 per cent of the shares can prove to be helpful when problems arise. It can provide an incentive or apply some pressure on management to perform. However, when such a company can have 25 per cent of the shares, that useful pressure can be translated into a dangerous threat. Therefore, I urge Members of the House to accept the argument, which was put to us by the President of the Canada Development Corporation, that it would make sense to accept the logic we have applied in the case of the banks with a 10 per cent shareholding and accept this constructive and straightforward amendment in the first block of amendments to be voted on.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to address a few remarks to this particular amendment. It should be noted that this amendment that was put forward by my colleague is his own amendment, unlike the others that will follow. They were really suggested by the President of the Canada Development Corporation while in committee.
The Hon. Member is correct in his analysis that the evidence which was adduced during the committee hearings with regard to the foreign investment factor in this particular Bill would lead one to conclude that a 10 per cent or perhaps 12 per cent or 14 per cent shareholding as would be more reasonable. The logic of the 10 per cent shareholding referred to by my colleague was echoed quite eloquently by the President of the Canada Development Corporation when we had an opportunity to cross-examine him before the legislative committee.
We also had an opportunity to cross-examine individuals of the divestiture committee of CD1C as well as officials of CDC and the Minister responsible. I believe that their arguments against the suggestion of foreign investment being less than 25 per cent-whether it is 10 per cent or the 14 per cent to which I alluded earlier-was practically null and void because on the subsequent day to the Minister's appearing before the committee, the President of CDC said that it was logical to live by the provisions of the Bank Act which provides for 10 per cent, and therefore why not provide for 10 per cent in this Bill?
While I rise to support the amendment, I also want to indicate my disappointment in the framework of the Legislative committees. I believe that those of us who have been in the Chamber for more than a year had hoped that legislative committees would function in such a way as to improve upon a Bill. However, when evidence was adduced from various sources in an attempt to improve the legislation, I say quite sincerely that we found to our dismay that Government Members were either under duress or some direction, which meant that the objective to improve legislation was not being achieved, notwithstanding that there had been a consensus about the new committee system of the House.
While we will support Motion No. 1, it was my hope that during our deliberations in the legislative committee there would have been a disposition by Members to recognize the benefits not only of the evidence which we put forward as Opposition Members but indeed of evidence put forward by individuals involved with CDC on a daily basis. They are the ones who have to live with this legislation in the market-place. Although they did not recommend it specifically, they found nothing inherently wrong with going to 10 per cent and felt that that perhaps would be the best way to proceed.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Under the proposed amendment, Mr. Speaker, a Canadian investor might be barred from holding more than 10 per cent of the shares. The Bill as drafted sets the limit at 25 per cent. In my opinion, this has been the subject of lengthy debates in committee and we came to the conclusion that if a shareholder could not acquire more than a token CDC share he might find himself in a position where he would carry little weight with the board of
November 22, 1985

directors who would then run the risk of keeping to themselves in their ivory tower.
When we considered the advisability of lowering the limit from 25 to 10 per cent, the main argument was that a 25 per cent holding might enable the investor to cash in his investment at consolidation value, which is important, and the other advantage was that no shareholder would be able to acquire all the shares. So there was an advantage on both counts.
Concerning the objections raised by my colleague from Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), I might remind him that the provisions of Clause 5(2) were mentioned on several occasions during committee proceedings, for they do establish mechanisms designed to stave off any prospective take-over by a group of shareholders. 1 would suggest that those clauses are good enough and would defeat any take-over attempt. With respect to the 10 per cent ceiling proposed under the amendment, I think the shareholders would be very hard pressed to participate fully in the activities of the CDC or convince management to steer a new course should it ever become advisable to do so. Therefore 1 am opposed to the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to say a few words about this particular motion. I listened with interest to the Hon. Member who just spoke, attempting to make a case for 25 per cent participation in CDC. Quite frankly, that debate has gone on in the House many times. 1 think the most obvious time that it occurred was in the last revision to the Bank Act. At that time witness after witness- and I cannot recall the exact number of witnesses who appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs-emphasized and re-emphasized the point that in something as critical as a bank, we needed at least a 10 per cent ownership rule. That simply ensures adequate participation so that there is not an overdue influence by any particular individual or group. I think 10 per cent is the general rule of thumb one would find not only in the Canadian banking system but generally around the world. It is considered to be a rate which provides for adequate participation in terms of corporate decision making and ensures a wide enough ownership base so that no individual, particular firm or particular group would have undue influence.
When the Government asks that this be 25 per cent, it goes against a trend with the new Government. The most obvious reflection of that trend was when the so-called Blenkarn report of the Finance Committee was presented. It was felt that all ownership provisions on financial institutions should be taken off; that if an Arab prince or an enterprising wealthy Hong Kong entrepreneur wanted to buy one of our major trust companies or banks, so be it; and that there was no concern about single domestic ownership, so much power in the hands of an individual, be he a Canadian or a foreigner. That betrays a rather interesting view of what is in the best interest of Canada and what is in the best interest of Canadian control of our financial institutions or other institutions.
Canada Development Corporation
It seems to me that there is a mind-set developing with the Government, saying that it has faith in the system, that if a single individual owns 25 per cent, that is fine; if a single individual owns the Bank of British Columbia, that is fine. Quite frankly, I do not think that is fine. I cannot imagine where one would find evidence to suggest that that is in the best national interest. Everything I have read, at least anything credible, would certainly indicate that that kind of concentrated financial, economic and therefore political power, seldom acts in the best interest of the country per se.
This is why the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) has put forward a motion indicating that the 10 per cent rule should be followed in the case of CDC as well. I think we should give serious consideration to this particular proposal. If we really believe in building in a sense of fairness and equity into the corporate sector, this principle would be maintained by following the provisions of this particular motion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments in support of the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). The motion, as has been stated, would simply reduce the percentage of shares which could be held by any individual or group in the reorganized CDC from 25 per cent to 10 per cent.
The Bill is aimed at the privatization of the Canada Development Corporation. We have not seen any real justification for that, but presumably the Government would want to say that it is to lead to greater competition and to a possibility where more Canadians would have the opportunity to participate in one of the 10 largest corporations in Canada. This year, the corporation has total assets of some $7.8 billion. If we want to see that greater diversification, at the very least we should support a motion such as this one which would limit the total shares that can be owned by any individual or group to a maximum of 10 per cent. That is a very healthy amount which can be owned by any individual, group or corporation. Ten per cent seemed like a logical upper limit, a very generous upper limit, if we are concerned about reducing the amount of corporate concentration in Canada. I am not sure that is what members of the Conservative Party are interested in. If they look at the effects of the Bill, they will see that it will lead to greater corporate concentration.
We would at least like the same type of protection built into the Bill as is in the Bank Act, where any individual is limited to a total ownership of 10 per cent of the assets.
On that basis, I urge Hon. Members opposite to take very seriously the argument put forward by my hon. colleague and to support the motion.
Motion No. 1 (Mr. Langdon) negatived.

Motion No. 2
That Bill C-66, be amended in Clause 5
(a) by striking out lines 5 and 6 at page 4 and substituting the following
therefor:

Canada Development Corporation
"forfeiture of dividends, the removal from or refusal of registration of securities and for the sale of securities held or beneficially owned in contravention of the constraints".
(b) by striking out line 5 at page 5 and substituting the following therefor: "sons, owns more than 20 per cent of the".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment that we have before us now is an amendment that comes to us directly from the board of directors of the Canada Development Corporation, which has reviewed this piece of legislation carefully. The board of directors appeared before the committee to give their judgment.
This is a privately, entrepreneurially run corporation, which will shape the future of that enterprise. The board recommended that we accept this amendment. They did so very specifically because they believe the Bill as it is presently drafted does not protect the independence of the CDC and the capacity of the CDC to do a job for the country as a whole.
The board talked to us in committee about various recommendations. 1 would like to quote to Members of the House from the testimony of the President of CDC, Tony Hampson dealing with this amendment. He said:
We also recommend that subclause 5.(2) be revised to provide CDC with authority to sell shares owned in continued contravention of the constraint provisions of this legislation.
1 asked Members of the House to follow this very carefully. He went on:
Without CDC having power to enforce a sale-
This is on the legal advice that CDC received. He continued:
-it would be possible for a shareholder to exceed the limits on share ownership and achieve control even though the excess shares could not be voted. For example, as now proposed, a non-resident investor-
This is not me speaking, but the head of the private corporation with whose affairs we are dealing in this Bill. He said:
-who accumulated 90.1 per cent of CDC's voting shares would have everything above 10 per cent neutralized;
That is, the last 80 per cent they could not vote but neither could anybody else vote those shares. Let me continue. He went on to say:
-but the unaffected 10 per cent holding would still outvote the shares held by all the remaining shareholders.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we are talking here about an extremely dangerous loophole in the Bill pointed out to us forcefully and unanimously by the board of directors of the Canada Development Corporation. They said that if we do not close that loophole and if we do not make it possible for the board to force those shares to be sold, which are held in contravention of the 10 per cent and the 25 per cent limitations, then they can be held on to. They cannot be voted, but because the company holds this vast number of shares, which it cannot vote plus a number of shares which it can vote, more than the remaining shares in the operation, it becomes possible for a single powerful company, either a foreign company or a single Canadian company, to take over the enterprise, despite the fact that the enterprise is set up to serve the country
widely, to meet employment needs across the country and to fill a great many different business needs.
CDC, as Members of the House know, is a holding company which has under its auspices such important businesses as Connaught Laboratories, producing insulin in Canada, Poly-sar, producing artificial rubber, Petrosar, producing specialized chemicals, and Kidd Creek Mines in northern Ontario, which has perhaps the richest concentration of lead zinc mines and smelters in the province. CDC is an important company. Yet the small technical loophole identified by the lawyers of the Canada Development Corporation leaves completely open the possibility that our purposes as a House in trying to build in some safeguards, safeguards that will keep this company Canadian controlled and will keep it subject to 25 per cent control, will be contravened.
This corporation could be subject to a back door raid which would take it out of the hands of people here in our country. It is not a loophole which would have jumped off the page to me as I read through the legislation, but it is a loophole which the corporate lawyers of CDC themselves take very, very seriously. It is a corporate loophole which the entire board of directors of Canada Development Corporation requested us as a Parliament to correct.
I hope that with that kind of support from the groups of people, who will hopefully make this company a success in the future, Members of the House will be prepared to accept the amendment which follows the wording proposed by the CDC board and will give CDC the protection which it requests from this kind of back door raiding practice.

Mr. Speaker, the proposal as suggested by Mr. Hampson, President and Chief Executive Officer of the Canada Development Corporation, would ensure that no one, or several affiliated companies if the parent company holds less than a 50 per cent interest in each of the subsidiaries, would be able to take control of CDC.
Anyone with any background in business knows that one need not own 50 per cent of the stock to control a company. In that regard the 20 per cent restriction which the President of the CDC proposed was, in my view, a very wise move to ensure that CDC does not become a puppet of other corporations. That, of course, would reduce the chance of having monopoly situations arise.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I believe it is actually Motion No. 2(a) with which we are presently dealing, or are we in fact dealing with (a) and (b)l
Both. They are lumped together.
I see.
1 hope that will not be taken off my time.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It won't be included because it was probably constructive.
November 22, 1985

As I said earlier, this particular amendment was suggested by the President and Chief Executive Officer of the Canada Development Corporation.
It was interesting to note that during the deliberations of the legislative committee, the President and Chief Executive Officer of the CDC came before the committee with the clear impression that it was his duty and moral obligation to present for committee members ideas and suggestions which he believed would improve upon the legislation without deviating from the Government's objectives. It was his clear understanding that he was to appear before the legislative committee to make suggestions and draw to the attention of members ways in which this Bill could be improved. He did make a number of suggestions and this is one of them.
Government Members, and particularly the Minister responsible, were of the view that if this amendment as suggested by the individuals who work on a daily basis with CDC was accepted, it would somehow interfere in a negative way with the prospectus which was offered earlier by CDC. That argument is a fairly substantive one. Government Members spoke of the right of rescission or damages if in fact there was an amendment made which would subsequently interfere with the prospectus. In that case, there is provision under the Ontario Securities Act for individuals to take action against the Government.
The President and the Vice President and General Counsel of the Canada Development Corporation came well equipped to the committee meetings. They retained the services of a very prominent and distinguished law firm by the name of Fasken and Calvin. This law firm spelled out very clearly that the amendments that were being sought by the officers who were entrusted with carrying on the activities of that corporation would in no way interfere with the prospectus, thereby giving right to individuals to activate the provisions of the Ontario Securities Act. A legal opinion was written by that very distinguished Canadian firm involved in the securities business. I quote from page 6 of this opinion which was filed for all committee members to read:
The proposed change in the definition of "associate" in the Bill to trigger associate status at 20 per cent rather than 50 per cent ownership of a corporation would not, in our opinion, give rise to contractual rescission rights.
That is very clear. Not only do the Chief Executive Officer and the Vice President and General Counsel of the corporation say that, but a prestigious and distinguished law firm says that those amendments will in no way destroy, defeat, impair or inhibit the objectives of the Government. It is merely a provision designed to improve upon the legislation.
It surely was the intent of the McGrath committee when it established the new rules for legislative committees that individuals would come before Parliament in a non-partisan manner to make suggestions to improve upon legislation. In this case, we have three clear and unequivocal examples of support for a particular amendment designed to improve upon the legislation.
What happened in committee? I do not want to rehash for all Members what happened in committee. However, the
Canada Development Corporation amendment was defeated. We are now trying to bring it to the attention of Hon. Members that surely there must be a time for Parliament to put aside partisan politics and accept the recommendations and legal opinions of the experts who are trying to achieve something that will be for the betterment and not for the detriment of the Government.
I do not want to jump to the conclusion that some backroom discussions have taken place with certain individuals. However, there is evidence to allow one to conclude that perhaps something of that nature has taken place over a period of time. The amendment sought by the President and Chief Executive Officer of the CDC is clear. He has a legal opinion to back up his submissions. I think in the interest of Parliament and in the interest of improving legislation, which 1 believe all of us wish to do, we should accept this amendment which has been offered by members of the Canada Development Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I will keep my remarks regarding this particular motion very brief in order to allow us to deal with them all today. I will confine my remarks, by and large, to Motion No. 2(b). This motion contains quite an extraordinary suggestion, one made by senior representatives of the CDC in order to guard against a very peculiar takeover potential.
I appeal to my colleagues opposite, many of whom understand and are active participants in the business world and know full well that in business as it is practised in Canada today, the 20 per cent ownership rule is considered quite usual and acceptable. Based on that assumption, I have a question to ask. I have to ask what on earth would motivate government Members to introduce the 50 per cent rule unless they plan to open up a loophole that would allow for back-door takeovers or the concentration of power.
I see that my friend, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer), is laughing at my concern over increased financial and corporate power in Canada and the falling of more and more power into the hands of restricted numbers of individuals. The Hon. Member might think that that is funny. With all due respect, he might find that humorous. However, when businesses like Cadillac-Fairview start warning us that a number of these practices will result in increased corporate financial and political concentration of power in Canada, I do not find it to be a laughing matter. I do not find that humorous. I do not find it at all encouraging in terms of the direction in which the country appears to be moving.
Not like Russia at all.

No. I guess my friend across the way is a supporter of the Soviet Union's system of economics. I will allow him to take his turn and explain. In a sense, I suppose we are moving toward more and more control being placed into the hands of a single individual, whether it be an individual entrepreneur, an individual business or perhaps even the state. The Conservatives are taking us into an interesting development these days. I do not know what they are using for their

November 22, 1985
Canada Development Corporation
models, perhaps the Bronfman group, the Laurentian group or maybe the role of Conrad Black. Perhaps they are using as their model some of the state governments in Eastern Europe, or perhaps even the Soviet Union. I do not know but 1 find the development ironic.
I would like to explain step by step what is really going on here.
This is incredible!

My friend across the way says that this is incredible. I agree that it is unbelievable in terms of what the Government is attempting to do. At the present time we have a situation in which firms and associate firms together can own more than 25 per cent. In other words, there is a 25 per cent rule in place. The associated firm is usually limited to a 20 per cent participation. The Government now wants to increase the 20 per cent participation level to a 50 per cent participation level. The point I am trying to make is that Brascan, which now owns 26 per cent of Noranda, could purchase 25 per cent of the CDC and Noranda could purchase 25 per cent of the CDC. Brascan literally controls Noranda with a 36 per cent ownership. The point is that right now Brascan and Noranda together could control 50 per cent of the CDC. Brascan already controls Noranda. We are saying that, in a sense, with the present proposal before the House, Brascan could control 50 per cent of the CDC. It could own 50 per cent of the CDC.
1 see my hon. friend shaking her head across the way. Perhaps she can explain where my logic is incorrect. If I am not incorrect and if the Government is saying it accepts the notion that Brascan can, should and may control 50 per cent of the CDC, then this is a dangerous signal to be sending out across the country. It concerns me very much.
Again, in its wisdom, management has suggested that we use the 20 per cent rule. I appeal to my business colleagues across the way to use the 20 per cent rule which is found in all aspects of prudent business practices in our country. Why is it that the 20 per cent rule is not being followed today? In a sense, a step is being taken which could quite easily and quite likely result in Brascan controlling 50 per cent and owning 50 per cent of the CDC. I have posed two or three questions to my hon. friend and I will sit down now and listen to her response.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to answer my hon. friend's question about concentration of power.
In speaking to the first amending motion, I referred to Clause 5(2) which gives to the Corporation, and protects certain powers that an ordinary corporation would not have. I think that what is already in the Bill provides that the Corporation will be able to protect itself against this kind of activity.
Mr. Speaker, the motion now under consideration is divided into two parts, and I would like to say a few words about each one.
First of all, in the motion numbered 2(a), we see that if the clause were amended, this would enable the Board of the CDC to sell all shares held by shareholders who failed to comply with the ownership provisions and to strike these shareholders from the Corporation's records.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to make the CDC a corporation under the Canada Business Corporations Act. 1 think that if we consider the amendments being requested, few businesses of this kind dispose of such powers of confiscation.
With this amendment, the CDC would be drawn even further away from the Canada Business Corporations Act.
As for the second half of the motion, its effect would be to create a partnership between two corporations if one of them, or the enterprises with which it is associated within the meaning of the definition provided in the same clause, own more than 20 per cent of the other corporation's voting shares. At the present time, the clause provides a ceiling of 50 per cent on ownership of shares of an associate corporation.
This proposal also has the same effect as the first part of the motion, namely that it goes against the purpose of the Bill which is to make the CDC as much as possible a corporation that would normally come under the provisions of the CBCA. Under this legislation, to control means to own more than 50 per cent of securities to which are attached votes that may ordinarily be cast to elect directors of the Corporation. This definition corresponds to what is provided in provincial legislation on corporations and securities and in the Bank Act.
Mr. Speaker, considering the fact that members of the Legislative Committee have had ample time to discuss this motion in committee and did not decide to adopt it, 1 cannot concur with this motion.

Mr. Speaker, again, I wish to urge Members opposite to look closely at the amendments put forward by my colleague and to consider the process in which we are involved. I ask them to consider whether or not we are really concerned about seeing wider ownership of the corporation or if we want to see much more concentration in the Canada Development Corporation.
It is interesting to note that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), pointed out in committee that four out of the seven members of the divestiture committee which was set up to look into the reorganization of the CDC were associated with Brascan. This gives weight to the questions which have been raised about the possibility of the Brascan group gaining control of the CDC.
It is important to remember that these amendments were first suggested by the board of directors of the CDC as an attempt to close a loophole which would permit one corporation, for example Brascan, to gain complete control of the CDC. This is quite apart from the present restrictions and what they are supposed to do. Under the loophole, one corporation can purchase more than 25 per cent of the shares even
November 22, 1985

though it would not be able to vote those shares. The amendment provides that the company would have the right to insist upon the sale of those shares held outside the restrictions which this Bill purports to impose.
The second part of the amendment would change the definition of an associate from one holding more than 50 per cent of the voting shares of the corporation to one holding more than 20 per cent of the voting shares of the other corporation. What we all recognize is that 50 per cent ownership is not needed for effective control of most corporations. Even 20 per cent gives control in many cases, particularly if other shares are widely held.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) asked the Minister a question in committee with respect to the situation regarding Brascan, Noranda and MacMillan Bloedel.
I would like to quote from the proceedings of that committee where the Hon. Member said:
Perhaps I could ask the Minister this question, to take a specific question. Forty-nine per cent of MacMillan Bloedel is held by Noranda Mines. It therefore does not come under paragraph (/) as an associated company. In your opinion, would MacMillan Bloedel be deemed to be associated under paragraph (jh) and therefore prohibited from buying a big chunk of CDC in addition to the 15 per cent or 25 per cent that Noranda may have?
The Minister responded:
Mr. Chairman, that is the type of thing I think if those circumstances arose ... Clearly, if the company were concerned, they would have to go to their counsel and ask for an opinion. Now, you asked me in the situation you have outlined to give an opinion. I do not intend to give that type of opinion. You have the clause here. There are paragraphs (a) to (h) dealing with the interpretation of what associate is with respect to the whole associated status in the clause itself.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), very properly pointed out that the Minister was in effect abdicating in saying they would have to go before the courts to determine what Parliament intended with this clause.
What we are trying to do with this amendment is to make it very clear that we do not want to see that kind of corporate concentration. We do not want to see CDC fall into the hands, or effective control, of only one corporation or one group of corporations. Hon. Members opposite are very concerned about what they would consider excess Government control of the CDC. 1 think they should be equally concerned about excessive corporate control by one corporation or one group of corporations. On that basis I urge those Hon. Members to look very seriously at these amendments and to support them.
Motion No. 2 (Mr. Langdon) negatived.

speechtext: We will now debate Motion No. 3 and Motion No. 4 together. They will be voted on separately.

Motion No. 3
That Bill C-66, be amended in Clause 8 by striking out line 9 at page 8 and substituting the following therefor:
"by-laws inconsistent with any such provision or continue the Corporation under the laws of any other jurisdiction."
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-66, be amended by adding immediately after line 9 at page 8 the following:
"9. The Corporation shall not sell, assign, transfer or deliver control of all or a substantial portion of its property other than
(a)	in the ordinary course of business or as security for a bona fide loan or other financial assistance; or
(b)	to an affiliate as defined in the Canada Business Corporations Act, of the Corporation and, if a sale, assignment, transfer or delivery of such control to an affiliate occurs, then such affiliate shall be bound by the provisions hereof."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the curious situation which leaves a New Democratic Member of Parliament acting as spokesperson for the Canada Development Corporation before the House is something which leaves me mildly embarrassed although, frankly, only mildly embarrassed because I think the CDC has, on balance, an excellent record in the contribution it has made to our development and to our independence. It has the capacity as well to withstand political pressure which was demonstrated so bravely during the past Government when the attempt was made to put Mr. Maurice Strong in as chairman of CDC and the present president of the CDC, Tony Hamp-son, fought that political incursion as energetically and as effectively as one could possibly hope to see from any private sector company worth its salt.
Therefore, 1 am actually one Canadian who is proud of the contribution which CDC has made to our country and 1 am one who looks forward to tremendous contributions from it in the future if it is safeguarded, its independence is protected and its management capacity to take risks, the long-term view and to look at our country as a place to grow in, is protected by us, the Parliamentarians of Canada.
With that in mind, 1 come to these last two amendments. So far we have been speaking about differences of opinion. We could have a 25 per cent limit or we could have a 10 per cent

November 22, 1985
Canada Development Corporation
limit. We have been speaking about the differences which might exist in defining an associate company and about the question of whether there is a loophole which exists in some of the existing wording, with some of us saying, yes, and some of us saying, no. Now we come to something which is far more crucial. It is a set of loopholes in the existing legislation which one could drive a rather large World War II blimp through. These are not loopholes you drive trucks through. These are massive loopholes. They are loopholes which open up the possibility that this whole Bill which we have painstakingly worked on could simply come to mean nothing to CDC because it is left open within the legislation that all of the CDCs assets could be transferred to another jurisdiction. At that point all of the safeguards which we have put into the Bill throughout our work in committee will simply disappear.
The Canada Development Corporation, perhaps, will be sold to South Carolina and the Carolina Development Corporation will from now on run Kidd Creek Mines, various chemical plants in Sarnia and the labs in Toronto which discovered insulin. It is possible that the assets could be sold into a different jurisdiction over which this whole Bill which faces us would no longer be applicable. Therefore we must have a clause inserted into the Bill to prevent that before it becomes law. The president of the Canada Development Corporation, speaking on behalf of the entire Board of Directors of the Canada Development Corporation, said that under the present wording of Bill C-66, the Council-that is the Council of Directors of CDC,-believes that there is nothing to prevent a future board of CDC, whether or not acting on behalf of a dominant domestic or foreign shareholder, from subsequently obtaining continuance in another jurisdiction but without the share constraints of Bill C-66, and that an amendment should thus be made to Subclause 8-2 to prevent CDC from being continued away from foreign jurisdiction.
I am not a lawyer, Mr. Speaker. I am not a businessman. I am not someone who regulates stock exchanges, thank God. However, I am someone who takes seriously the measured words of one of the most respected businessmen in this country when he says this Bill is not going to be worth a hill of beans if we do not close some of these loopholes. He even comes forward and says here is precisely how we can do it. He is giving us precise wording which will not benefit CDC itself, but will benefit us as parliamentarians in putting forward legislation which we would not want to see become the laughing-stock of this country. Therefore I plead with Members opposite, as part of a new approach to the analysis of legislation, to look very, very seriously at and accept this small amendment from the CDC board. Accept it not because it comes from us but because it comes from the CDC.
Further, I would argue that Motion No. 3 is complemented by Motion No. 4 which says that:
The corporation shall not sell, assign, transfer or deliver control of all or a substantial portion of its property-
Again, outside the country. This is very straightforward and I wish the committee had accepted it. I trust it would have accepted it had it not been for the unfair pressure by the Government saying that it had already put out a share issue and if we make changes in this Bill it will damage that share issue. It would make it possible, the Government said, for people to sue the Government because the details of the share issue are different from those of the legislation when it is passed. Therefore, I urge Conservative back-bench Members particularly to take seriously this message from one of the most prominent, indeed one of the best of the private corporations we will have in the future. I ask them to resist this blackmail message from the Government that we cannot change this legislation in even a tiny respect simply because the Government inappropriately, improperly and immorally placed a share issue on the market this summer before any of this had come before this House for discussion. I hope that those deeply persuasive arguments, based as they are in the tenets of firm Ontario Conservatism, will somehow have an effect on my fellow Members today.

Mr. Speaker, again I rise to speak to these two motions which, although not consequential, are in many ways interrelated. The arguments we received in committee for rejection of the amendments put forward by the CDC were much in line with what I said regarding Motion No. 2: Somehow the amendments being put forward would interfere and give rise to civil actions under the Ontario Securities Act because a prospectus had already been issued and any changes or amendments to the Bill would be a material change and therefore the provisions of the OS A would be applicable. Unfortunately for the Government, a legal opinion obtained by senior members of the CDC disputed that statement regarding this particular measure. This amendment, if approved by the Government, would not, as the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) said in giving evidence before the committee, be a material modification to the Bill.
It seems to be quite logical that this amendment falls in with the objectives the Government initially announced regarding this legislation. The Government is restricting ownership of the shares in that only 25 per cent can be held by foreign interests. There is a certain make-up or splitting of the shares. However, the Act is silent on the continuance of the corporation in another jurisdiction. It was interesting to read the testimony of the senior legal counsel for the CDC who said very clearly that in his view he was not seeking a major amendment. 1 think 1 am quoting him correctly and if I am not, I am sure Government Members will jump to his defence. This amendment just seems so logical given the objectives and thrust of the Bill. 1 assumed from our deliberations, when he made his comments and saw the amendment, that he thought it would follow and follow very quickly. Unfortunately, once again, we saw in the legislative committee a stonewalling by Government Members notwithstanding the judgment of outside legal counsel, the chief executive officer of the corporation, Opposition MPs and
November 22, 1985

researchers that we understood very clearly the logic of this amendment.
It does not make sense that under the Canada Business Corporation Act you have certain restrictions but when you give the corporation the opportunity to continue that legislation under another jurisdiction the provisions we have all talked about, the restrictions on the shares, no longer are applicable. It seems to me to be a fairly substantial loophole. I cannot understand it, particularly when we heard the Minister himself say what he hoped to achieve by way of the CDC. What he has argued for in this Bill goes out the window because the Government refuses to put in a clause regarding continuance under another jurisdiction.
My colleagues to the left who have mentioned various corporations could, perhaps, argue that a deal may be coming down of which we are not aware. However, Mr. Speaker, that is only speculation or, as your predecessor would say, obiter dicta. When you lack logic or reason, when you lack legal, expert, or business opinion which says that what the Government is doing is correct, it leads one to conclude that perhaps there is some justification for being really concerned as to where the Government is going with this particular piece of legislation. I think the Parliamentary Secretary has handled this particular piece of legislation fairly well. Surely she and her colleagues can see the merit of the amendment unless, of course, what we saw displayed at committee is, in fact, what is taking place within the boardroom and the administration of the CDC; that the left foot does not know what the right foot is doing and the Minister does not know what either foot is doing.
I have no hesitation in supporting this amendment but it surprises me greatly that the Government has chosen to act with some degree of irresponsibility with regard to the provisions for the continuance of this corporation in another jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, this is a particularly important amendment. I am sure that Government Members will support it once they have had a chance to clearly evaluate the motivation behind it. It was recommended by a number of witnesses who suggested that this was in fact the appropriate step to take. If we fail to accept this amendment, there is more possibility that the CDC could be transferred into a totally new and different jurisdiction. To put it bluntly, Mr. Speaker, with the present legislation the possibility does exist for CDC to find itself under the jurisdiction of a province or perhaps even a foreign government.
I remember my hon. friend, the Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) speaking out for many, many years on the concern that is being raised by Hon. Members that we might lose the ability to benefit, through our own regulatory system, from these kinds of economic endeavours. I would expect him to have some words to say on this motion for sure.
Canada Development Corporation
One wonders what hesitation the Government has in accepting an amendment which keeps the CDC within the Canadian federal jurisdiction. As I understand the motion, it does nothing more than that. It is not that we assume that there are all sorts of bogeymen out there prepared to take immediate advantage of what may be a loophole, but, nevertheless, that possibility exists. People who understand the role that the CDC plays in the country and ought to be playing in the future are concerned that we close off the possibility of transferring the jurisdiction of a corporation so important to the development of Canada, even with its restricted powers. We must ensure that it remains within the federal jurisdiction, closing off the possibility for the control of power to be transferred to a provincial or even foreign jurisdiction. Once again, Mr. Speaker, I urge my Conservative colleagues to endorse this motion put forward by my friend, the Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to speak to the Motion No. 3, whose purpose is to prevent the federal Government from losing jurisdiction over the CDC.
Mr. Speaker, if we take a closer look at Bill C-66, we see that clause 5.1(d) already provides that the articles of continuance shall contain: "provisions respecting the enforcement of the constraints imposed pursuant to paragraphs (a) to (c); According to sub-clause 8(2), the Corporation "shall not amend any provision included in the articles of continuance in compliance with any of paragraphs 5(1 )(o) to (c) or make any articles or by-laws inconsistent with any such provision."
Therefore, if the Corporation came under a provincial jurisdiction for instance, it would nevertheless have to meet the requirements concerning ownership already provided for under this Bill.
Motion No. 4 deals with the sale of assets under extraordinary circumstances as defined in the Canada Business Corporations Act which states that any sale that does not occur in the normal course of business must be authorized by a special resolution calling for at least a two-third majority vote.
The CDC is a holding corporation and its assets are made up of shares from other corporations. The normal activity of such a holding is to dispose of these shares from time to time.
The constraint as proposed could create a certain ambiguity concerning the powers of the CDC to administer assets and make it impossible for the Corporation to act in the best interests of its shareholders. Strictly applied, it could freeze the CDC in its present structure. This would go directly against the interest of the shareholders who are now interested in the CDC because it is involved in share investments and will improve and rationalize its portfolio to maximize its profitability.

November 22, 1985
Canada Development Corporation
In view of what is already provided for under the Act, Mr. Speaker, I must oppose the proposed amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this amendment to the legislation before the House. It seems as though you were ready to ask the House to vote on this measure. Due to the importance of this measure, it is important that we give it more consideration and not sweep it through the House quickly.
My colleague proposed this amendment to the legislation in order to remove some of the glaring weaknesses in it. It is foolhardy and even tragic that the Government should seek to weaken and destroy the Canada Development Corporation which was originally founded in order to increase the control of the Canadian economy by Canadians. Since the major manufacturing industries of the country are owned by foreign investors it is important to have as many public policy tools as possible which enable us to strengthen Canadian control of the Canadian economy. Without Canadian control of the economy, Mr. Speaker, our political sovereignty is a hollow shell.
Canadians call upon Members of Parliament day after day to provide for their basic human needs, to remove the indignity of unemployment from the community. There is no way in which we can effectively respond to those appeals from Canadians for action without having control of our own economy. As long as the Canadian economy is controlled in New York in the headquarters of multinational corporations rather than on Canadian soil, there is no way in which we can effectively meet the needs of Canadians and respond to their cries for help. It is shameful that the Government is moving to weaken Canadian control of our economy at a time when we need to have control over it in order to provide for the needs of our people. The Conservative Government seems to have sold out the notion of Canadian control in the interest of worshipping the free market idol. It believes that if everything is left at the hands of the market-place and every decision is made by the private sector, the needs of Canadians will somehow be served.
Our Party recognizes that competition, in its proper place, can play a useful role and that the private sector has an important task to perform in the Canadian economy. However, the private sector with its private firms cannot serve its purpose in the Canadian community without being given direction by the Canadian people through the instrument of representative Government. Therefore, we hope that the Conservatives will abandon their ideological blinders and realize that if we are to have a genuine Canadian economy we must have control of Canadian industry.
It is important for us to have effective public policy instruments that will allow us to increase Canadian ownership of Canadian industry. Instead, the Government is weakening those instruments that will achieve Canadian control and is giving control of our economy to the private sector. It is
handing the future of the Canadian economy to individual firms and multinationals and abandoning its responsibility for steering the Canadian economy in a direction that will provide employment and serve the interest of Canadians.
Large multinational firms have their own interests. They seek to make a profit and expand. While those interests sometimes serve our national interests, it is not always the case. Unfortunately, there is an assumption with the free market ideology that the interests of private firms will always be the interests of the community. That is simply not the case. It has been proven by the Canadian experience. We know that in an economy such as ours, with a large percentage of manufacturing owned by foreign investors, employment in Canada is exported to the parent firms in the United States when there is a downturn in the economy. It is no longer acceptable to Canadians to suffer the vagaries of economic downturns and to have a lack of control of the Canadian economy. That is why we support the Canada Development Corporation and have suggested amendments that would strengthen the legislation before us in order to allow ownership of the CDC to stay in Canadian hands and continue to be an instrument of public policy.
Why would the Government want to weaken the CDC? Why would it want to weaken an instrument it has to ensure Canadian control of the economy? I can only assume that the Government is blinded by its own ideology and belief that prosperity can only be achieved through the free market system. The free market system is important as long as it serves the community interests. However, in order to achieve this, we must have public policy instruments that will ensure that the private sector serves the public interest. That is why we have moved these amendments to strengthen this legislation. That is why it is important to increase Canadian control of the economy rather than abandon that objective.
Motion No. 3 (Mr. Langdon) negatived.

Motion No. 4
That Bill C-66, an Act respecting the reorganization of the Canada Development Corporation, be amended by adding immediately after line 9 at page 8 the following:
"9. The corporation shall not sell, assign, transfer or deliver control of all or
a substantial portion of its property other than
(c)	in the ordinary course of business or as security for a bona fide loan or other financial assistance; or
(b) to an affiliate as defined in the Canada Business Corporations Act, of the corporation and, if a sale, assignment, transfer or delivery of such control to an affiliate occurs, then such affiliate shall be bound by the provisions hereof'.
Motion No. 4 (Mr. Langdon) negatived.
