speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged today to take part in the closing debate on Bill C-66 which will pave the way for the sale of the Government's Canada Development Corporation shares and the continuation of this privatization process.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) would have liked to have been here to express his own views on this Bill. Unfortunately, that was impossible.
Bill C-66 went through all stages quickly, but with proper consideration. This turn of events attests to the over-all support of the House as well as the efficient and stimulating manner in which it was dealt with. Most Hon. Members endorse the CDC privatization in principle, which happens to be a major element of the policy we announced in the May Budget.
Briefly I should like to go over the main provisions of the Bill. As I said, the first consideration is the transfer of federally-owned CDC shares to private interests. First and foremost the Canada Development Corporation is one of the major companies on our national market and it will now be able to operate on the same footing as other similar conglomerates. Under the existing CDC statute only Canadians may be shareholders, and no individual or group is allowed to own more than 3 per cent of the shares. Once the Bill becomes law, these restrictions will be more flexible and any Canadian citizen will be able to buy up to 25 per cent of the shares.
In the case of non-residents, 10 per cent will be the individual limit but such shareholders as a whole will not be permitted to own more than 25 per cent of CDC shares.
It has been suggested that a 25 per cent limit for Canadians is too high and would allow a single person to gain control of the CDC.
It has also been pointed out that there should not be a limit on the number of shares and that people should be able to buy and sell them like those of any other company. A ceiling of 25 per cent was chosen by the Government to reflect the balance needed to prevent a concentration of shares and to give certain
Canada Development Corporation shareholders the opportunity to play a more active role in the corporation. The conscientious debate we had on this issue in Committee confirmed the acceptability of the proposed limit.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it was also important to allow the CDC access to foreign capital while preserving its Canadian nature. On this point also, opinions were sharply divided. The Government set this ceiling based on similar provisions in the Bank Act. The limits provided in this Bill as concerns the ratio of shares held by non-residents alone or as a group will enable us to limit at three to one the proportion of Canadian and foreign shareholders.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, what we are doing today is a very important part of the mandate of our Government since we are providing for the eventual privatization of a public corporation. I believe that Bill C-66 has now received the consideration it deserves, for which 1 am grateful to my colleagues on both sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, first I pay tribute to the Parliamentary Secretary who has shepherded this Bill carefully forward in the period since the Minister's illness. Today is her accomplishment in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!
None of the criticisms which I will now go on to make are directed at her personally.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps you should look at me when you are speaking.

That is true. Let me start with the basic point at issue here. There are many ancillary points and side-issues, such as the procedures which the Government has followed, the question of Brascan and so on. I will talk about them, but they are side-issues.
At the heart of our concern about the piece of legislation has been a Canada Development Corporation which will be able to play a creative role in the future, similar to the creative role which it played in the past.
Many Hon. Members of the House were not Members when the Bill was first introduced. At that point, 1 had the privilege of being a member of the press gallery. I recall the sense Of delight at seeing an initiative taken that would try to create something which, at that stage back in 1970, was absent in Canada-the creation of a highly entrepreneurial business-oriented corporation in an attempt to fill the gap that is so apparent to us.
Canadian capitalism has had its weaknesses historically. That is why 55 per cent of our manufacturing industry is foreign owned. It is not because foreigners have come here and preyed on us like some kind of creature from the deep. They have come here because we invited them, and we invited them

November 22, 1985
Canada Development Corporation
because we did not have powerful, risk-taking private companies which were able to push forward various developmental ideas across the country. It is partly because of that gap and partly because of that absence that I am a social democrat rather than a Conservative. In other countries and in other places I could as easily, with the kind of respect I have for the contribution wheih private sector enterprise can make, have been a Conservative. However, in Canada, with the weakness of our capitalist sector, we have required Government leadership and support to build strong agencies of development. Historically we have needed them, whether we are talking about our history of railway building, our history of building the broadcasting system or our history in the 1970s of building an entity in the private industrial sector like CDC which would become a dynamic, effective, independent private firm.
That independence is important because it is an independence which permits the company-and Tony Hampson has talked about this, and I give him respect for it-to take a longer view. It can take a view which says that we do not have to get back our profitable returns within five years, that we do not have to look at each project which comes before us as a possibility as something that will be a money spinner in five years or six years, and that we do not need high discount rates on projects which will permit us to launch investments. It can take a view which says that we are prepared to look at the long shot, that we are prepared to take some chances, that we are prepared to take some risk, and that we are prepared to believe in our country and in the capacity of our country.
That is something which Hon. members on all sides of the House have learned to respect about the CDC over the years. There was a time when the CDC might have looked like another Liberal creation to pension off some political hacks who could not make it elsewhere. However, Tony Hampson prevented that from happening. He said: "No matter how good Maurice Strong is, he is a political appointment; he is not a businessman, so I won't have him".
The consequence has been a business which has proved itself. It has not proved itself as a great money-maker. CDC will never be a high-flyer in the business world, because it believes in looking at the long run and at taking some risks. It believes in the future of the country and in building that future step by step.
We have to recognize that there are concerns now as a result of the piece of legislation that that contribution to the future of the country, that commitment to the long-term view and that willingness to take risks, will be threatened, reduced and perhaps ultimately eliminated.
The workers in the industry are concerned. I have a letter before me from the Energy and Chemical Workers Union which was written to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) in which the union says:
The Energy and Chemical Workers Union is concerned about the possibility of the so called "privatization" of the Canadian Development Corporation and in particular its holdings in the Polysar Petrosar Development in Sarnia.
We believe that Polysar has developed a viable, sensible and uniquely Canadian multinational Corporation which is of value to all of Canada and all Canadians.
We believe that part of the reason for its development in the manner that has been achieved has been because of the support and approach taken by the Canadian Development Corporation. Polysar has developed into the world's largest synthetic rubber manufacturer and has a marketing network throughout the world that is second to none.
We believe that you should not disturb the type of relationship that our country has with any artificial change such as the so-called "privatization" of the Canadian Development Corporation. We believe that Canadians have been well served by the Organization as it stands and we think it should be encouraged and fostered in its present structure and not permitted to be moved into a new and artificial relationship within the Canadian corporate structure.
Yet that is what is taking place, Mr. Speaker.
This past summer, the Canada Development Investment Corporation, CDIC, recommended specific ways in which CDC should be opened up more to the influence and control of other private sector companies, other corporate empires in Canada.
When a share issue was put before the market in conditional terms this past summer, almost 15 per cent of the shares of CDC ended up falling under the control of the Brascan group, a group which itself had before that approached CDC and asked CDC whether it would be willing to join into a partnership between the Kidd Creek Mine in northern Ontario and Brascan's Noranda mining interests. This would have resulted in a significant reduction in competition in Canada. That is all on record in the committee hearings.
CDC said: "No, we want to keep our independence and our operation, providing as many jobs and as much competition as possible in northern Ontario". Brascan Noranda as a group holds almost 15 per cent of the shares and there is the possibility by this Bill that the percentage of shares could be increased to 50 per cent, because Noranda is not considered an associate of Brascan by the definition in the Bill, despite the clear, clear evidence in the corporate world that Brascan does control Noranda. We could find CDC controlled very much by Brascan because it has been established under terms set down by the CDIC divestiture committee which itself is dominated by four of its seven members from the Brascan group.
It is a rather sad, tawdry example of conflict of interest, unfortunate to see staining this Bill before us here in the House of Commons but it is the reality.
Let us take a look at that CDIC divestiture committee. One member of that committee is Trevor Eaton, President and Chief Executive Officer of Brascan. He is also a member of the board of Noranda. I remind Members that the divestiture committee not just only sets the regulations for privatization but came to us and testified in contradiction to the CDC itself, putting its weight as a divestiture committee directly and powerfuly into the legislative process, despite the fact that it is dominated by the very enterprise that would benefit by these takeover provisions.
Our records indicate that Mr. Marshall, a second member of that CDIC divestiture committee is the President of Bras-cade, another subsidiary of Brascan, another member of the board of directors of Brascan and a member of the board of
November 22, 1985

Noranda. A third member of that CDIC divestiture is Pat Keenan who is also a director of Brascan. A fourth member, A. Turmel is a director of Noranda. We have four out of the seven people on this committee dominating that committee who come from the very set of companies which will benefit from the rules set up with respect to the privatization provisions of CDC. This is a stained and tawdry side to what could have been a straightford privatization that many of us would have supported.
What is worse is the process by which this Bill has been brought before the House of Commons, as I indicated to the speaker this morning, has been at best something that can be called improper by the people to whom we referred the Bill at the Library of the House of Commons. The process has been described as having followed improper procedure.
We have a Bill in which the Government, before the Bill had even been considered at all by the House of Commons, issued a prospectus which had the details not of the present law governing CDC but of this new law. The Government then used the fact, blackmail, that share instalments had been sold to tell us in committee that we could not fully and freely consider amendments that were brought forward, because any amendment which had any substance to it at all would have the effect of giving to those shareholders, who had bought in instalments, the right to sue the Government of Canada for misleading them during that summer period when the share instalments were originally issued. As a new Member of Parliament, to consider that I am creating legislation with that kind of axe hanging over my head, with that kind of unfair, undue and unjustified pressure facing the committee and with that kind of explicit point brought before us by Government lawyers and the Minister, I for one do not find this to be the way parliamentary consideration of legislation should take place. I for one was not elected by the voters of Essex-Windsor to simply rubber stamp legislation which the Government tells us we cannot change because it has already taken steps based on the proposals that are before the House. Governments should not act in that unfair manner.
To sum up my argument, there are serious threats to the independence of this company, an important company for the future of Canada. There are clear threats coming from Brascan and Noranda. There are threats coming from the companies that themselves dominated four out of seven positions on the CDIC divestiture committee which shaped the details of this Bill.
We in the House have not had a chance to consider these various detailed points without pressure and without being pushed by the Government because of its past improper action leading unfortunately to what I have to consider to be a shameful piece of legislation over which we in the House of Commons will hang our heads in the future. We could have done it better. We should have done it better. Canada and the CDC would have been far better off if we had done it properly rather than under the pressure of a Government that is acting
Canada Development Corporation
in a far too high-handed manner for a Government yet so young.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of words to say concerning this particular piece of legislation. I think everyone will agree that the Government of Canada is bringing in this legislation in this fashion because it has a philosophy which was proclaimed during the election campaign and re-established by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and that philosophy revolves around getting rid of Crown corporations and having Crown corporations play a lesser role in the economy than they did previously. Of course, there have been contradictions to that philosophy.
The people of eastern Canada were somewhat surprised to see the Government announce recently that it would create a Crown corporation to run CN Marine. People wondered where the Government's philosophy went. They wondered why the Government was creating a Crown corporation when its policy was against the creation or existence of Crown corporations. The reason the Government created that Crown corporation was to save some $20 million through layoffs.
It is not so much the actual policy of the Government about which we are concerned but it is the way in which it carries out its policy. When doing away with the CDC, the way in which the Government does this has a lot to do with whether or not it accepts the doing away with that Crown corporation. For example, does the Government allow foreign investors to have shares valued at 25 per cent? That is one good question. Why would the Government sell the shares at a time when those shares would be valued at less than their proper value?
We are removing an instrument that existed within the system to assist Canadian industries that were in trouble at times. The Canada Development Corporation has stepped in many times over the years to be of assistance to certain sectors of our economy. Coming from eastern Canada, I think particularly of the fishing industry. As all Hon. Members know, the CDC played a very important role at various times in that particular industry. We have seen that situation change. The CBC was involved in financial problems of the fishing industry and then another Crown corporation called Fishery Products International, partially owned by both Governments and by the private sector, was created.
The Government's philosophy of carrying out its mandate by getting rid of Crown corporations just does not make sense in some cases. No matter which way we look at Crown corporations and the measures brought in by the Government, we are looking at layoffs. We are looking at layoffs at a time when layoffs should not be taking place.
We can take a look at the involvement of the CDC and the Government in the fishing industry. A recent announcement was made that the Government would put $100 million into Fishery Products International which operates on the East Coast of Canada. At the same time, the Government announced that it would close down 15 communities in which

November 22, 1985
Canada Development Corporation
there were fish plants. Why did the Government announce that?
This particular branch of the fishing industry had been invested in by the CDC. Then another Crown corporation was created in order to try to keep the fish plants open. The Government Crown corporation had a social responsibility to the people who lived in those communities, to the workers there and to the very existence of those communities. The Government came through with money, yes, $101 million, but then it agreed that 15 communities should lose their fish plants. In other words, the Government indicated in its press releases that it would get rid of the unprofitable fish plants and sell those to private enterprise. The Government said publicly that it would sell unprofitable operations to the private sector. Someone in the private sector would have to think twice before investing in something that is not profitable. The entire procedure that was used was absolutely ludicrous. Then the Government set a time limit of two or three years on some of the sales. Then the Minister rose in the House to say that we did not know if these fish plants would close because if they did it would be perhaps two or three years down the road.
I would like to congratulate a certain Member of the House who just happens to be a Progressive Conservative Member. I think that he deserves some credit in that he was able to salvage a fish plant that was due to be closed in his riding. I am speaking of an Hon. Member who sits opposite and represents the South Coast of Newfoundland. The philosophy of the Government of Canada is wrong. In saying that you will create a Crown corporation or allow it to continue as long as it saves money and as long as there are lay-offs, you can then turn around with the same philosophy and same standard and say: "All right. If you have a Crown corporation which is in trouble because of tariffs from another country we do not really want to get involved in that. That Crown corporation still has to break even".
I am thinking about the Canadian Saltfish Corporation having tariffs imposed against it. The Government could simply wipe its hands clean and say that that is the policy of the United States Government and the Canadian Saltfish Corporation will have to sink or swim. It must be realized that the Saltfish Corporation covers only a certain section of the coastline in the country, namely, the north shore of Quebec, all of Newfoundland and Labrador. In this case tariffs are imposed against a Crown corporation which competes against a private enterprise which does not have the same tariffs imposed against it. It is quite logical for one to see the inequity in that particular system. It surprises me that the Government would take that attitude since it is not only my riding affected but the riding of the Prime Minister.
The list goes on. We can consider the case of the CBC in this regard. The budget of that corporation was just cut. It was told that it would have to live within certain confines. It was told to make decisions now with respect to what it would close
down and cut off in terms of its programming but it must live within certain guidelines.
I do not disagree with the philosophy of this piece of legislation. I do not disagree with it at all. However, I do disagree, as do members of my Party, with the way in which it was undertaken and the timing with which it was presented. I disagree with certain provisions of the Bill. We have all heard of the suggestions made by experts in the field who have suggested amendments. The Government has turned around and has said that it will ignore those amendments. Whereas I agree with the general principle of the Bill 1 will have to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise and say a few final words with respect to this Bill. To make it perfectly clear to Hon. Members, I do not want to talk out the Bill. I believe there is an understanding that we will wrap up the proceedings this afternoon with respect to the Bill.
However, I do wish to put on the record a few final comments. We are dealing with Bill C-66, an Act respecting the reorganization of the Canada Development Corporation. We have heard a considerable amount of debate which was intended to point out why this particular move of the Government is an inappropriate one. I wish to back up for a few moments because people often ask: "What problems are we facing today?" They ask why it is that Canada seems to have such a difficult time not so much getting back on the track but simply on to a track. I do not think we want to go back on to the old track because that did not seem to be taking us any particular place. We want to get on to something new, a new track, a new development. We want to see the development of some new vision and the unfolding of new programs in order to get us there.
People often ask me what the problem is. They ask me: "Why is it that other countries seem to be able to do so much better? Why is it that other countries seem to be able to have an economy which thrives and develops as opposed to what has recently taken place with respect to the shoe industry in Canada?" The Government is cutting off the quotas with respect to shoes which means a few thousands workers will be put out on the street. What I am concerned about is that while we are simply cutting off workers in the shoe industry we have nothing to offer them in lieu of this abandonment. It seems to me that if the Government is phasing out quotas over a period of time that it would be more appropriate for it to phase in another program so those workers would have something to look forward to. They could be retrained in other areas. However, the Government is simply hacking off the quota system and saying: "That is the way it is. That is the invisible hand of the market-place about to play its role." That is really problematic.
Obviously, one has much to say about Bill C-66. 1 believe it would be appropriate to allow the Bill to continue on to its eventful demise, in terms of the progressive motions and amendments we have put forward. I will sit down and save my comments until another time.
November 22, 1985

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As Hon. Members are aware, on this day's Order Paper there are three motions in amendment at the report stage of Bill C-79.
Motion No. 1 seeks to impel the Government through the CDIC to make cash advances to the uninsured depositors of the financial institutions in a different manner than that which is envisaged by the Royal Recommendation attached to the Bill. It appears to the Chair that this is an imposition on the financial initiative of the Crown. In this regard, I would refer Hon. Members to Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation No. 540.
Also, the Hon. Member's motion seeks to offer an alternative scheme to that contained in the clause, which cannot be done. I would refer Hon. Members once again to Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation No. 773(9).
Depositors Compensation
Motions Nos. 2 and 3 will be debated together and a vote on Motion No. 2 will dispose of Motion No. 3.
1 see that the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is not in the House. Is there unanimous consent to have the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) move the motion on her behalf?

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (for Miss Nicholson (Trinity)) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-79, be amended in Clause 12 by adding immediately after line 35 at page 6 the following:
"(3) Notwithstanding the Bank Act, the Minister shall cause to be published in this year's Public Accounts a list of all depositors to which a payment
was made under this Act."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reason for the introduction of this motion is pretty clear. It is that we do not know who will receive the funding which the Government proposes. In other words, we all know of the system which is in place in the country which will pay depositors when we have a situation such as that of a bank failure. People may be reimbursed for their deposits up to the sum of $60,000. Those people are insured under the provisions of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. We know that system and that it is in place in this country. It is a safety mechanism so that Canadians can feel assured that when they do put their money into a financial institution they will be reimbursed if there should be financial problems with that particular institution. However, the Government of Canada is not only going to pay the amount of money which legally has to be paid under the Deposit Insurance Program, but those depositors who have money in the bank far above the limit will now also be reimbursed by the Government. We have to realize the difference between the first insurance program announced by the Government and the other insurance program which has always been in place. The difference is quite simple. In the first instance of the Deposit Insurance Corporation, a fee is paid by the bank on the amount of deposits which are held in that particular bank to the tune of a percentage of 1 per cent. That is how that fund is maintained. If the Deposit Insurance Corporation happens to get into financial difficulties and has to overdraw that account-in other words, if it is costing more than is being sustained by the payments through the banks-then, of course, there would be a deficit in the account. We all know there is a deficit there now, perhaps to the tune of just over $1 billion give or take $200 million or $300 million. Then, of course, the Government supplies the funds directly to the Deposit Insurance Corporation to make those payments. We have, therefore, a self-sustaining fund. The Minister will have to bring in a Bill increasing the percentage of pay-in by the banks because of the deficit position of the Deposit Insurance Program.
However, what we are talking about in the second insurance program is a decision by the Government of Canada to make enormous payments. In some cases these payments will be made to organizations which represent a lot of people and

November 22, 1985
Depositors Compensation
everyone can see that that certainly is warranted. Also included in that list are individuals, foreign interests and people who perhaps put enormous amounts of money into the bank for a particular financial reason at a particular moment in time. Why, then, is the Government strapped into this? It is because the Government, through the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), made a clear statement to the people of this country that there was no problem at all with the Canadian Commercial Bank. This Bill is before us because there was established a moral obligation on the part of the Government to bring in this particular Bill to pay off those depositors who had enormous amounts of money in that Bank. In other words, the Government brought in a Bill to bail out a bank saying that the Bill will do the job. Thereby, in its statement and its actions it morally committed itself to do what it is doing now.
Most people would agree with the pay-out which would go to certain organizations who represent a lot of people. However, who disagrees with releasing the names of those people who will receive the millions and millions of dollars? Surely, there is a principle involved here. This is the taxpayers' money. How can the Government hand out money in the form of a cheque without saying who it is giving the money to? What organization, credit union or group of people would say that they did not want their names released to the public?
The Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance said that the reason they could not give us the names of those large depositors is because it violates the secrecy provision of the Bank Act. But where is the bank? Does the Bank Act cover the Canadian Commercial Bank right now? Will it cover the Canadian Commercial Bank in six months' time, in one year's time or in two years' time? When we have no bank in existence, how is the secrecy provision of the Bank Act an excuse for not releasing the names of those people, some of them multimillionaires, who will receive taxpayers' money from the Government? The Government turns around and says: "Oh, no. We are not going to let you know who these people are". However with the Freedom of Information Act, one can get the name of a fisherman who has been paid off for his salmon licence by this Government for $500. According to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance, however, we cannot get the names of the people who will receive these large amounts of money.
That is basically the reason for the amendment which has been proposed by the Official Opposition critic on this particular matter. It is a simple matter of saying that if we are going to do an extraordinary act, we must justify it to the taxpayers of this country. It matters not why we had to do that act. We all know why the Government had to do it. It was because the Government made an error. It made a political judgment which was a tremendous error. I am not going to stand in this House and say that the error was the responsibility of the Minister of State for Finance. She was not present when the decision was made for the bail-out and therefore, she personally is not morally responsible to pay off all of the rich people, the foreign investors and all of the organizations which had
money in that bank. Neither is the Minister of Finance morally responsible. He was not at any of the meetings when the decision was taken to bail out the banks thus committing the Government to that moral obligation. In fact, we do not know who was responsible for that decision. All we can do is guess. The person responsible for committing this Government to a moral obligation to pay off people who had more than $60,000 in this bank, we suspect, is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
We suspect there was a phone call which went from someone in the Alberta Government to the Prime Minister and the decision was made against everyone's recommendation. It was made against the recommendation of the banks which participated because the bank representatives have said so. Everyone washed their hands of the decision. The decision was made, we suspect, by the Prime Minister, who made himself a moral obligation on behalf of the Government to pay off foreign investors, and multimillionnaires, using the taxpayers' money, without releasing those names to the taxpayers. That makes absolutely no sense whatsoever. My time has expired but perhaps I can continue this interesting discussion at the next sitting.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Surrey-White Rock-North Delta) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should recognize the historical significance of former political leaders by adopting a policy of naming buildings and significant chambers or committee rooms after them, thereby recognizing their contribution to Canada.
November 22, 1985

He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank Members of the House for the interest they have shown in this motion. The idea for this actually began several months ago when 1 was taking part in Canada Day celebrations in White Rock when all of us at that meeting were expressing our appreciation for our heritage and the opportunity to foster an appreciation for that heritage.
Communities across Canada are light-years ahead of our national institutions in giving recognition to leaders in their communities who have contributed to the cultural and historical wealth of that community. I had to point out during those ceremonies the irregular way in which Parliament has handled the recognition of political leaders here in Ottawa with respect to the naming of buildings or erecting of monuments to their honour. 1 pointed out that we on Parliament Hill have used all of our imagination to name some of our buildings. There is one building we call the East Block. Isn't that great? Isn't that imagination? Then we went even further, and on the opposite side of Parliament Hill we named the building the West Block. There is imagination. Does that not tug at your heart-strings? When we bought the Wellington Building we reached deep into the soul of our nation and called it the South Block. All the while the tourists and school children come to Ottawa to visit Parliament Hill to see these institutions and what do they hear? East Block. West Block. South Block.
We tend to wonder why Canadians do not have an appreciation for their history. Our neighbours to the south are at times jingoistic or chauvinistic about their history but we are just the opposite. We tend to depersonalize our history at every turn. In our Charter of Rights and in much of our legislation we want to present ourselves as being interested in the individual, the human being. However, when we come to our history, we try to depersonalize it as much as possible. Therefore, I want to emphasize the fact that here on Parliament Hill we ought to be laying the cornerstone of appreciation for our heritage, our history and our traditions.
That is the background to the motion I have presented, Mr. Speaker. The fact is that our people have a textbook understanding and appreciation of our history. It is not a human understanding. What would it be like if school children visiting these buildings, instead of hearing East Block, West Block, Room 209, Room 269 or Room 371, they were to hear the names of historical leaders of our country who have contributed so much to our welfare and well-being today? I am not for the present trying to assign names to buildings or committee rooms, but I am asking the Government to take the initiative and assign the responsibility to a relevant group to make sure that we recognize those people in our history who ought to be remembered for their contribution and assign their names to the relevant buildings and committee rooms.
For example, on Parliament Hill we give no recognition, beyond perhaps a monument, to our first Prime Minister. Would it not be appropriate, for example-and I say only for example-that the East Block, which houses the original Cabinet Room and offices of the first Prime Minister, as well as the offices of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to name that building the
Naming of Committee Rooms
Sir John A. Macdonald building? Would it not be appropriate to name the West Block after Sir Wilfrid Laurier, our great Prime Minister from the turn of the century who really guided our country through 12 or 15 very important years for our nation? Would it not be appropriate that what we now call the South Block or the Wellington Building be called the Sir Leonard Tilley Building? He was one of the Fathers of Confederation who, incidentally, gave us our national motto. As a reward for that gift he has practically been forgotten.
An Hon. Member points out that off the Hill there are buildings named after historical figures. Is that not ironic? There are buildings named after key historical figures across Canada but on Parliament Hill we forget them. We have the Sir Guy Carleton Building downtown, as well as the C.D. Howe Building. But on Parliament Hill we ignore them. Why not name the room where the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration meets, after Mr. Sifton who really changed the course of history by introducing imaginative immigration policies which opened up western Canada? Why not name the room where the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs meets after Sister Marguerite Bourgeoys, that great pioneer of health care in the City of Montreal in the 1700s? She was a trail-blazer and the only place you can find Sister Bourgeoys is in the history books or if you go to the east end of Montreal. Would it not add something to the history of Canada if, as school students come up on the Hill, they hear that a committee room has been named after Sister Bourgeoys? They would ask why the room was so named and the guide would have an ample opportunity to go into the historical significance of and contribution by this great person. Why not name the room where the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture meets after George Brown who founded one of our great newspapers and added to the communications system of our country?
I do not want to take up much of the time of the House but 1 wanted to leave with the House an understanding of what we could do to personalize history by naming our buildings and many of our committee rooms after those historical figures who have contributed so much to our country. I believe that there is general agreement among the Parties to accept this motion as a direction for the Government. There may be other speakers who want to contribute to the debate but, if there are not, I would ask for the relevant motion to be put.

I do not think there is anyone in the House who could disagree with it in principle. Maybe the Member can think about that.

November 22, 1985
Naming of Committee Rooms
Certainly we recognize that there are distinguished Members from all political Parties who could very properly receive recognition, either by having a building named after them or a room in one of the buildings. Perhaps some of the more difficult rooms to find in the West Block could be named after some of the Members who are seldom found in their seats in the House. Maybe they have been lost there all these years. It is hard to say.
I can think of a number of people whom I would like to see so honoured. I think of Agnes Macphail, J. S. Woodsworth, Tommy Douglas, David Lewis, Stanley Knowles and M. J. Coldwell as well as people from other Parties.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext: How about Louis Riel?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext: Well, Louis Riel was a distinguished Member of this House. He did not distinguish himself in the House as much as he did outside, but he was certainly a distinguished Member of the House and I think he is generally recognized now as being a great Canadian. 1 would, however, like to ask the Hon. Member who would make the decision as to what building is going to be named after whom.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext: The Government in power.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext: Someone over there said "the Government in power", and that is the very concern that we have. There must be some kind of an arm's length procedure developed in order that this would not simply become the equivalent of a Senate appointment or another form of patronage. I think all Members would agree that the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson was a great Canadian and a worthy Canadian after which to name either a building or an airport. However, those of us who sat in the last Parliament remember the bad taste that was left in our mouths when the Toronto International Airport was named after Lester B. Pearson because it was done in such a way that its prime function seemed to be to enhance the fortunes of the Liberal Party in Toronto. Being a good Liberal, Mr. Pearson, perhaps looking down from Grit heaven, may not want to have it any other way. I do not know.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext: You mean looking up.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL HERITAGE NAMING OF BUILDINGS AND COMMITTEE ROOMS
speechtext:
I do not wish to get involved in a discussion of our three-story universe as our terminology obviously betrays us. I think it is very important, if we are going to name buildings after people, that we do not descend to the type of procedure which leaves people feeling other than good about the name that is used. We want the name to honour the building as well as the building to honour the name. We also want to have a sense of appropriateness. The Hon. Member
who spoke before suggested some possible names. The John A. Macdonald Building for the East Block seems reasonable. Due to the number of Private Members' Bills presented by people who want to bring back the noose, 1 was wondering which of the present Tory Members might want to have a future gallows named after them.
On a more serious level, Mr. Speaker, I think we all recognize what the Hon. Member said about Canadians having a sense of history and wanting to have some public recognition of that. On that basis, I am very happy to support the motion and would urge that any provisions made to implement it would be at arm's length from the Government to avoid any hint of patronage.
